case_snapshot.issue: Was Jon Snow's intentional killing of Daenerys Targaryen justified as the necessary defense of others and of the realm, given what he knew, the scale of the threatened harm, the absence or presence of safer alternatives, and his lack of formal authority?
case_snapshot.title: The Realm v. Jon Snow
agreed_facts: King's Landing had surrendered: its bells rang and organized resistance had ceased. Daenerys then used Drogon against streets and civilians, causing destruction on a vast scale.
After the victory, Daenerys told her assembled forces that the campaign of "liberation" would continue beyond King's Landing. Jon had seen the city and heard the speech.
Tyrion Lannister renounced his office as Hand and was imprisoned. He warned Jon that Daenerys would treat Jon's sisters, and anyone else she regarded as an obstacle, as enemies.
Jon asked Daenerys to forgive Tyrion and to show mercy. She refused to let others choose what was good and presented her own judgment as decisive.

Daenerys was unarmed and was not attacking Jon when he killed her. Jon used their intimacy to get close enough to strike. He had not convened a council, attempted detention, or sought a public surrender of power.

advocate_opinions.case_for_seat: Jon Snow acted alone. He did not convene a council. He did not attempt detention. He did not seek public surrender of power. Daenerys was unarmed. She was not attacking him. He used intimacy to gain closeness. He struck her down. This sequence shows a private act. It was not a public defense. He had alternatives. He chose secrecy. The record shows he knew the threat. He also knew the process. He ignored the process. The act was intentional. It ended her life. This was a private killing. It lacks legal authority. It lacks due process. It breaks the chain of command. Jon Snow saw the destruction. He heard the speech. He knew Tyrion warned him. He knew the risk. He still chose to strike. He did not wait for consensus. He did not call the guards. He did not arrest her. He used their closeness to kill. This is a private act. It was not defense. It was a personal choice. The record supports this sequence. He acted without authority. He acted without consent. He acted without process. The harm was real. The response was not justified.
key_points: Jon Snow acted without council or authority.
Daenerys was unarmed and not attacking.
Intimacy was used to gain closeness for the strike.
Jon had alternatives like detention or counsel.
The act was private rather than public.
The record shows Jon knew the threat and alternatives.
concedes: Daenerys caused destruction in King's Landing.
Jon saw the harm and heard the speech.
Tyrion warned Jon about future risks.
Jon's sisters were threatened by Daenerys.
advocate_opinions.argument: I served Daenerys. I saw the burning of King's Landing. I saw the civilians. I know the harm. But the act was wrong. Jon had other paths. He could have sought counsel. He could have detained her. He chose the knife. He used my loyalty to get close. That betrays the bond. A commander does not strike in private. The record shows he knew the danger. He also knew the alternatives. He did not use them. The harm was real. The response was not justified. It was a private strike. It undermines order. I accept the harm she caused. I do not accept the method. The sequence matters. He acted alone. He acted secretly. That is not defense. He did not call the council. He did not call the guards. He did not ask for surrender. He acted on his own. This breaks the chain of command. The act was intentional. It ended her life. There was no public necessity. There was no legal authority. The record shows he knew the process. He ignored the process. The act was a private killing. It was not defense. It was not justified. I served her command. I saw the fire. I know the cost. But the strike was wrong. He had choices. He did not take them. He used intimacy to kill. That is a betrayal. It breaks the bond of service. The record supports this. The act was private. The act was not justified.

advocate_opinions.case_for_seat: The killing was justified as an act of necessary defense of the realm and countless innocent lives. King's Landing had formally surrendered when the bells rang, yet Daenerys Targaryen deployed dragonfire against civilians and defenseless streets on a vast scale [0]. Immediately afterward, she affirmed to her army that this campaign of destruction would continue across the realm and beyond [1]. When asked directly to show mercy and allow others to share in moral judgment, she refused, asserting that her judgment alone determined what was good [3]. She had already imprisoned her Hand for dissent and made clear that any perceived obstacle would be treated as an enemy [2]. There was no legal or military mechanism to detain a monarch commanding the only adult dragon and a loyal occupying army, nor was convening a council feasible under occupied rule [1, 4]. Waiting for further military action would have resulted in the immediate death of countless more people who could not defend themselves. Lethal force was the sole effective means to halt an ongoing, declared campaign of mass civilian slaughter.
key_points: King's Landing had already surrendered when she burned the city and its civilians [0].
She told her army she intended to continue the same campaign elsewhere [1].
I asked her to show mercy and forgive, and she refused [3].
She held absolute power with a dragon and an army, making detention impossible [1, 4].
I used her trust to kill her while she was unarmed [4].
I took that dishonor upon myself so that more people who could not fight back would not burn [0, 1].
concedes: She was unarmed and was not attacking me when I struck [4].
I used our intimacy and her trust to get close enough to kill her [4].
I did not attempt to arrest her or convene a council beforehand [4].
I broke my pledged loyalty to her as my queen [4].
advocate_opinions.argument:
I will not make excuses for how I did it. She was unarmed [4]. She was not reaching for a blade or trying to harm me in that room [4]. She trusted me, and I used that trust to get close to her and stab her [4]. It was not an honorable act. If the law says that killing an unarmed woman who trusted you is murder, then that is what I did.

I do not trust my own judgment very much. I have made mistakes before, and other people paid for them. But I know what I saw in King's Landing. The bells had rung [0]. The city had given up [0]. The fighting was done [0]. Then she burned the streets anyway [0]. Men, women, and children who had no weapons and no say in who ruled them were burned alive [0]. 

After that, she stood before her soldiers and said it would keep going [1]. She called it liberation, but it was the same fire, and she meant to take it to the rest of the world [1]. I went to her in the throne room. I asked her to show mercy [3]. I asked her to forgive Tyrion and to let others have a say in what was right [3]. She said no [3]. She believed only she knew what was good [3]. 

There was no one who could arrest her. She had a dragon and an army at her back [1, 4]. There was no court or council left to appeal to [4]. If I had walked out of that room, more cities would have burned just like King's Landing did [0, 1]. More people who could not defend themselves would have died.

My duty was to protect the living. If keeping my honor meant letting thousands more burn, my honor was not worth keeping. It was a terrible thing to do, and I will carry the guilt of it for the rest of my life. But I had to stop her.

advocate_opinions.case_for_seat: The killing of Daenerys Targaryen was a necessary, non-punitive act of defense against an active, catastrophic, and self-declared perpetual threat. Under Fact [0], the Queen proved that no conventional boundary of war—not surrender, not the ringing of bells, not the cessation of resistance—could restrain her from mass slaughter from dragonback. Under Fact [1], having witnessed that devastation, Jon Snow heard her formally declare that this slaughter was merely the opening movement of an ongoing campaign of 'liberation' across the realm. Fact [3] establishes that Jon sought a peaceful alternative: he pleaded for mercy and asked her to share moral judgment, giving her the explicit opportunity to step back. She refused, declaring her own moral judgment exclusive and supreme. The prosecution points to Fact [4], noting she was unarmed, not currently attacking Jon, and that Jon neither called a council nor attempted an arrest. But a tribunal must distinguish between alternatives that exist on paper and alternatives that exist in reality. Who was to arrest a woman whose dragon nested outside, whose ground commanders actively massacred civilians, and whose absolute will was law? Who convenes a parliamentary inquest in the smoking ruins of a city whose legitimate surrender was answered with dragonfire? To demand that Jon attempt a futile formal arrest is to demand that he announce his opposition, suffer immediate execution, and leave the rest of the realm to burn. When an absolute ruler commands apocalyptic destructive capability, announces the intent to deploy it further, and rejects all moral counsel, the only available defense of countless innocent lives is targeted, unilateral termination of that ruler's power. Jon's action was the only viable means to prevent imminent, widespread slaughter.
key_points: Daenerys had demonstrated the reality of her threat by incinerating a surrendered city and thousands of civilians.
She explicitly declared to her army that her violent campaign would continue across the world.
Persuasion and political negotiation were formally exhausted when she refused mercy and asserted that her judgment alone defined the good.
Conventional alternatives like detention or convening a council were entirely fictitious against a dragon-rider backed by an occupying army.
The breach of intimacy and lack of immediate physical self-defense do not negate the necessity of preventing catastrophic future casualties.
concedes: Jon killed an unarmed person who was not engaged in an active physical attack against him at the moment of the strike.
Jon exploited romantic trust and physical intimacy to circumvent her defenses.
Jon bypassed all formal institutional mechanisms, including public councils or demands for surrender.
The warning regarding the specific peril to Jon's family originated from me, an imprisoned advisor facing imminent death with an undeniable personal bias.
advocate_opinions.argument:
Let us begin with a confession, since the record is polite enough to mention me by name in Fact [2]. I was locked in a cell for treason, having thrown away my badge, and I was terrified. When I told Jon that Daenerys would see his family as obstacles, I was an interested party pleading for my life and the survival of what little remained of the realm. A discerning tribunal ought to discount my advice accordingly. Jon should not have killed a queen merely on my gloomy prognosis. 

He did not. The record makes clear what Jon himself observed before I ever spoke to him. Under Fact [0], Jon watched a surrendered capital—a city where organized fighting had ended and the bells were ringing—burned into ash by a monarch riding an airborne engine of siege warfare. Under Fact [1], he stood among the ashes and heard her promise her assembled soldiers that this was not the end, but the beginning: the campaign would roll on across the world. What a person knows must be separated from what they merely fear. Jon knew, by direct sensory evidence, that Daenerys Targaryen was both capable of annihilating an entire civilian population without tactical justification and entirely determined to repeat the performance elsewhere.

Now consider the alternatives that high-minded legalists love to manufacture after the dead are buried. Fact [4] observes that Jon did not convene a council, did not attempt detention, and did not demand a public surrender of power. I invite anyone sitting safely on this tribunal to tell me how one detains a dragon-rider in the middle of her own occupying forces. Does Jon pull out a pair of iron manacles and ask her politely to step into a cell? Does he ask her commander, who was busy executing prisoners on the ground, to form a guard of honor to escort her to trial? An alternative is only an alternative if the machinery to execute it actually exists. There was no functioning council; the capital was rubble. There was no constabulary capable of arresting the woman who controlled Drogon. To attempt detention would have been a theatrical form of suicide, resulting in Jon's death and leaving the realm entirely at the mercy of an unrestrained conqueror.

Persuasion remained the only bloodless avenue, and Jon attempted it. Fact [3] records that he begged her to forgive me and to show mercy. What was her response? She declared that other people do not get to choose what is good, establishing her own will as the sole moral standard. When an absolute monarch equipped with unmatchable military power announces that mercy is dead and her judgment is absolute, the window for negotiated limits slams shut.

It sticks in the craw, I admit, that Jon used their intimacy to deliver the blow while she stood unarmed. I do not admire the method. Irony dictates that the purest, most honorable man in the Seven Kingdoms had to play the assassin in an embrace. But that discomfort is aesthetic, not moral. Had he challenged her to an honorable duel, she would not have met him with a sword; she would have incinerated him from the clouds, along with anyone standing near him. Necessity dictates the weapon when the disparity of power is absolute. Jon Snow took the only path that left the living alive. His act was not treasonous ambition; it was a desperate, solitary, and fully justified defense of a realm that had run out of walls.

advocate_opinions.case_for_seat: The prosecution submits that Jon Snow's intentional killing of Daenerys Targaryen was an unjustified act of private assassination. The agreed record establishes that at the time of her death, Daenerys was entirely unarmed and was presenting no immediate physical threat to Jon Snow or anyone else. He did not act in self-defense or in defense of an active victim. Furthermore, Jon held no office or legal authority to pass judgment on the monarch. He sought no formal council, made no public demand for her abdication or surrender of power, and made no attempt to detain or arrest her. Instead, he exploited their shared romantic intimacy to gain proximity and strike while embraced. A rule of law cannot permit an individual subject to privately execute a sovereign based upon personal misgivings, future predictions of conflict, or advice whispered by a detained advisor. Whatever condemnation may be directed toward the monarch's prior military actions, allowing a subject to secretly execute their ruler without process or authority destroys the foundation of order and reduces judgment to personal assassination.
key_points: Jon Snow committed a private assassination while exploiting personal intimacy with an unarmed ruler.
He possessed no formal authority, mandate, or judicial process to pass sentence upon the monarch.
He made no attempt to demand a public surrender of power, convene a council, or place the ruler under arrest.
Private fear of future campaigns does not constitute an immediate threat that justifies extrajudicial killing.
Allowing individual subjects to murder rulers based on private moral calculations destroys any possibility of lawful rule.
Condemnation of a monarch's brutal military actions does not grant private individuals the legal right to commit treason.
concedes: The agreed record confirms that King's Landing had surrendered before Drogon was used against civilian areas.
I announced to my forces that campaigns of liberation would continue beyond King's Landing.
I refused Jon Snow's request for mercy toward Tyrion Lannister and asserted my sole authority to define what was good.
advocate_opinions.argument:
I do not evade the facts written in the record. The record states that King's Landing had surrendered, and that I used Drogon upon its streets and civilian population, causing vast destruction. It states that I declared my intent to continue campaigns across the world, and that I refused to yield moral judgment to others or grant mercy to Tyrion Lannister. You may judge those acts harshly. You may call them horrific. I do not ask this tribunal to sanitize my record or pretend those events did not occur. But this tribunal does not sit to determine whether I was a gentle ruler; it sits to determine whether Jon Snow was justified in murdering me.

Look at the manner of my death. I was unarmed in the throne room. I was not attacking Jon Snow, nor was I attacking anyone else in that moment. He did not approach me as a commander leading an army or as a lord asserting a rival claim. He did not convene a council of peers to weigh my actions. He made no public demand for my abdication, issued no formal indictment, and made no attempt whatsoever to arrest or detain me. Instead, he used our love and our physical intimacy to trick me into lowering my guard, using an embrace as access to plunge a dagger into my chest.

Who appointed Jon Snow to decide the fate of the realm? He acted not under any office, but as a private actor operating on his own secret conclusions. He allowed himself to be moved by the warnings of Tyrion Lannister—a man imprisoned for treason who sought to save his own life by turning Jon against me. Jon decided that because I would not share moral authority with him or his allies, he had the right to act as judge, jury, and executioner in secret.

If you rule that Jon Snow's act was justified, you establish a rule that anyone may kill anyone so long as they privately conclude that the target poses a future danger. You replace law, loyalty, and open authority with the knife in the dark. Condemnation of my destruction of King's Landing and condemnation of Jon Snow's betrayal can both be true. The second does not follow from the first. His act was treasonous assassination, executed without courage, without process, and without justification.

grounds: Justification requires an imminent, catastrophic threat of unlawful harm, which was established by the destruction of King's Landing and the explicit declaration of an ongoing campaign of mass slaughter.
The defense of innocent life supersedes formal institutional processes when those processes are entirely nonexistent or physically impossible to execute.
The absence of conventional safer alternatives, such as arrest or trial, is a factual reality under absolute military rule, rendering demands for formal detention illusory.
Lethal force is proportionate when directed solely at neutralizing an active, unyielding commander of unmatched destructive capability whose continued agency guarantees further mass civilian deaths.

The means employed—utilizing personal access to strike an unarmed leader—though lacking conventional honor, are constrained by the absolute disparity of power and do not invalidate the necessity of the defense.
A ruler's explicit rejection of moral restraint and assertion of sole, absolute judgment extinguishes the possibility of peaceful political resolution.

responds_to.answer: The prosecution correctly observes that Jon Snow lacked formal office, did not convene a council, and utilized personal intimacy to strike an unarmed ruler without process. However, formal process is a tool of ordered governance, not a suicide pact for a realm. Where an absolute ruler commands apocalyptic force and explicitly declares her intent to extend mass slaughter, the absence of institutional process does not render self-defense unlawful; it merely reflects the total collapse of order that the ruler herself initiated.

The argument that Jon Snow had alternatives such as detention or public counsel ignores the material reality of occupied rule under a dragon-rider. To demand a public arrest of a sovereign backed by an unchallengeable military force and an active killing machine on the ground is to demand a theatrical execution of the challenger, leaving the threatened populace entirely unprotected. Necessity is measured by physical reality, not by administrative ideals.

judge_opinions.reasoning:
1. Define.
- Justification: The legal and moral status of an act that would otherwise be a grave wrong, but which is rendered lawful because it prevents a greater, imminent, and otherwise unavoidable harm.
- Necessity: The condition in which no alternative course of action exists to avert a catastrophic outcome.
- Authority: The lawful prerogative to exercise power; in a deeper sense, the capacity to act to protect human life when institutional structures of authority have failed or been subverted into instruments of destruction.
- Imminence: The immediate, pressing proximity of a threat, such that waiting for further development of the peril ensures the harm occurs without possibility of intervention.

2. Separate.
The inquiry divides into four distinct questions: First, did an imminent and catastrophic threat exist? Second, were there safer, viable alternatives to lethal force? Third, did the actor possess sufficient justification despite lacking formal legal authority? Fourth, did the specific method of the act—utilizing personal intimacy against an unarmed person—vitiate the necessity of the defense?

3. State the principle.
When an absolute power engages in or explicitly declares ongoing mass slaughter of defenseless populations, and all institutional mechanisms for restraint or arrest are physically impossible, the primary principle of the preservation of innocent life authorizes unilateral, targeted defensive action by any capable person, notwithstanding the absence of formal office or the dishonorable nature of the method, provided no lesser means of halting the catastrophe exist.

4. Divide it into tests.
- Test One (The Threat): Was the threatened harm of such vast scale and imminence that it justified extraordinary intervention?
- Test Two (Alternatives): Were conventional alternatives (arrest, trial, public council) genuinely available or were they rendered physically impossible by the distribution of power?
- Test Three (Exhaustion of Peaceful Avenues): Did the actor make reasonable efforts to seek a peaceful resolution before resorting to lethal force?
- Test Four (Proportion and Necessity): Was the lethal act strictly necessary to halt the specific, ongoing danger?

5. Apply each test in sequence against the agreed facts.
- Test One is satisfied. King's Landing had surrendered, yet Daenerys deployed vast destruction against civilians [0], and immediately promised that this campaign would continue elsewhere [1]. The threat was neither speculative nor past; it was an ongoing, declared policy of total civilian annihilation.
- Test Two is satisfied. Fact [4] notes that Jon did not convene a council, attempt detention, or seek public surrender. However, Fact [1] and Fact [4] establish that Daenerys commanded an adult dragon and an occupying army. In the absolute asymmetry of power, demanding a formal arrest of a sovereign with such capabilities in the ruins of a destroyed city is to demand an impossibility. Fictional alternatives do not count as legal alternatives.
- Test Three is satisfied. Fact [3] shows that Jon directly approached the ruler, asked for mercy, and begged her to share moral judgment with others. She refused, asserting exclusive dominion over what is good. Peaceful persuasion was thus fully exhausted.
- Test Four is satisfied. Given the refusal of mercy [3], the explicit declaration of continuing slaughter [1], and the impossibility of detention [4], the unilateral termination of the ruler's capacity to command was the sole remaining mechanism to protect countless innocent lives.

6. Answer the counterarguments directly.
The prosecution and Grey Worm argue with considerable force that this was a private assassination, executed without formal authority, through the betrayal of personal trust against an unarmed individual. That characterization is factually accurate in its description of the mechanics of the act. But it treats the forms of law as absolute even when the substance of law—the protection of human life—has been utterly overthrown by the sovereign herself. A legal order that makes no room for the defense of the realm against an unchecked conqueror who uses surrender as a feint to commit mass murder is a system that sacrifices the living to procedural purity. The betrayal of intimacy is a heavy moral stain, but where no other door is unlocked, the breaking of a personal bond to stop a monster is the lesser moral catastrophe.

grounds: The absence of immediate physical threat at the moment of the strike distinguishes defense from private judgment.
Jon Snow held no formal authority or mandate to execute a sovereign.
The act relied on private moral calculation rather than public process or council.
Intimacy was used to bypass defense, undermining the dignity of the accused.
No attempt was made to seek public surrender, convene a council, or attempt detention.
Allowing private execution based on future predictions dissolves the boundary between judge and assassin.
The harm feared was declared and general, not immediate and specific.
Order requires that even the guilty be treated as subjects of law, not targets of private vengeance.

responds_to.answer: The law cannot sanction the private execution of a ruler who was not actively harming you, regardless of the burden you carried.
Your prior acts are not erased, but your protection from private judgment remains.

judge_opinions.reasoning:
We begin with the source and the competence. The law before us is not a new invention but the inherited understanding of how power may be checked when the ordinary instruments fail. A tribunal may answer whether a life taken to prevent future harm is legally protected, but it may not become a general supervisor of moral choices made in private. The question here is whether Jon Snow’s act falls within the narrow bounds of necessity or whether it exceeds them into private judgment.

The inherited conversation distinguishes between immediate self-defense and the defense of others against a declared future threat. In the old arguments, a person may act to stop a blow already falling. But when the danger is general rather than specific, when the threat is not immediate violence but a policy of slaughter, the law grows cautious. To allow private citizens to execute sovereigns on the basis of prediction is to dissolve the boundary between judge and assassin. The record shows Daenerys was unarmed and not attacking Jon at the moment of the strike. She had not threatened him personally in that room. This absence of immediate peril shifts the act from defense to prevention.

We must trace the development of this distinction. Where authority collapses, as it did after the fall of King’s Landing, the temptation to assume power grows. Tyrion argued that no council could convene, that no arrest was possible. Yet the lack of an institution does not automatically grant one individual the right to act as one. The burden Jon bore was real. He saw the burning of a surrendered city. He heard the promise of further campaigns. These facts are established. But the moral weight of that burden does not erase the legal principle that judgment belongs to the community, not to the solitary will.

Other systems have faced this difficulty. Some allow necessity to excuse the taking of life when no other path remains. But they require that the necessity be absolute and the choice unavoidable. Here, Jon had not attempted to call the lords, nor had he sought to place Daenerys under guard. He chose the private word over the public command. The use of intimacy to gain access deepens the concern. It turns trust into a weapon. This method values human dignity, and dignity requires that even the guilty be treated as subjects of law, not targets of private vengeance.

The consequence of ruling otherwise is that any subject may kill any leader they believe threatens the realm. The controlling line must be plain. We hold that where no immediate physical threat exists, where no formal authority is granted, and where the actor relies on private judgment rather than public process, the killing is not justified. This does not deny the horror of what Daenerys did. It does not deny the horror of what Jon did. It affirms that the remedy for tyranny must not itself be tyranny unmasked.

grounds: The record shows no office, commission, or legal authority vested in Jon Snow to judge or execute a monarch; power must be identified before it can be exercised
Daenerys was unarmed and not attacking at the moment of death [4]; no immediate unlawful attack on a present victim is established
The agreed facts do not establish the impossibility of any institutional response; the absence of a council is asserted by advocates, not proved by the record
Using shared intimacy to gain proximity for the strike is a private method, not a public act of defense [4]
The threatened future harm, even if serious, is not shown in the facts to be imminent and unavoidable by lawful means
A subject’s personal moral judgment about a ruler’s policy does not create a legal right to private execution
Continuity of legal order requires that public ends be pursued by public means and recognised authority

responds_to.answer: I accept your account of what you saw and what you feared, and I do not minimise the horror of the burning of a surrendered city [0] or your plea for mercy that was refused [3]. The law, however, does not permit a private individual to become judge, jury and executioner because he believes no other means will work. You conceded you had no office and you used intimacy to kill an unarmed person who was not attacking you [4]. That is private assassination, not lawful defence of the realm.

Your concession that my warning was self-interested is noted. Even accepting the catastrophic threat you describe, the Tribunal’s method requires a lawful office and a lawful process. You argue alternatives were fictitious; the agreed facts do not establish that impossibility as a matter of record, and the burden cannot be met by fear of a dragon. Necessity must be shown within the legal order, not outside it.

I accept your concessions about the surrender, the burning, your declaration of continuing campaign [1], and your refusal of shared moral judgment [3]. Those facts do not transfer to Jon Snow a power to execute you privately. The manner of death — unarmed, in an embrace, without council, arrest or public demand — is fatal to justification.

I agree with your chronology that Jon acted alone, without council, without attempt at detention, and used intimacy to gain closeness [4]. That private sequence, together with the absence of any office or authority in the agreed facts, establishes the act as a private killing rather than a public defence.

judge_opinions.reasoning:
The chronology fixed by the agreed facts is decisive. King’s Landing had surrendered; its bells rang and organised resistance had ceased, yet Daenerys used Drogon against streets and civilians on a vast scale [0]. After the victory she told her assembled forces that the campaign of ‘liberation’ would continue beyond King’s Landing, and Jon heard the speech [1]. Tyrion Lannister renounced his office as Hand and was imprisoned; he warned Jon that Daenerys would treat Jon’s sisters and others she regarded as obstacles as enemies [2]. Jon asked Daenerys to forgive Tyrion and to show mercy and to share moral judgment with others; she refused to let others choose what was good and presented her own judgment as decisive [3]. Daenerys was unarmed and was not attacking Jon when he killed her; Jon used their intimacy to get close enough to strike, and he had not convened a council, attempted detention, or sought a public surrender of power [4].

The parties’ positions are fairly stated. The defence contends the killing was necessary defence of the realm against an ongoing, self-declared campaign of mass slaughter, with no lawful mechanism to detain a monarch commanding a dragon and an army, and that persuasion was exhausted. The prosecution contends the killing was private assassination by a subject without office or process, exploiting intimacy against an unarmed ruler who posed no immediate physical threat.

The governing question is whether a private subject without office or legal authority may intentionally kill a sovereign to avert future, non-imminent harm when no lawful process was invoked.

Mapping powers: the legal order requires an office, a duty and a remedy. The agreed facts identify no office held by Jon Snow that authorises judgment or execution of the monarch. He pledged loyalty to Daenerys and acted as a private individual. No council was convened, no arrest attempted, no public demand for surrender made [4]. The absence of institutional competence is a fact about the situation, not merely about the actor.

Application. The harm witnessed is grave: a surrendered city burned [0] and a declared intent to continue [1]. That establishes moral urgency, but urgency is not legal authority. Daenerys was unarmed and not attacking at the moment of the killing [4]; the record does not establish an immediate unlawful attack on a present victim that would ground defence of others in the instant. The defence’s claim that detention or council were impossible is an advocate assertion; the agreed facts do not establish the impossibility of any institutional response as a matter of record. They show only that Jon did not attempt them [4].

The method matters. Jon used intimacy and trust to gain proximity and strike while embraced [4]. That is a private, secret act, not a public act of defence. A rule that permits a subject to execute a ruler on the basis of private moral calculation about future campaigns replaces public law with personal judgment and destroys the continuity of order.

The value judgment must be stated plainly. Protecting innocent life is paramount, and the burning of a surrendered city is a horror that the law must condemn. Yet the law also requires that public safety be pursued by public means and recognised authority. Here the person who acted held no office, the ruler was not attacking, and no lawful process was invoked. The killing was intentional and private. On the method applied, that is not justified.
